## Abstract

Physical education (PE) programs play an important role in promoting physical health among youth, yet curriculum design is often guided by tradition and personal preferences rather than empirical evidence. This study examines the relationship between standards-based PE knowledge and self-reported physical behavior outcomes among high school students, using a cross-sectional dataset collected from 1,504 students across 9 Indiana secondary schools during the 2018-2019 academic year. Knowledge was evaluated using a 39-item assessment based on the three knowledge-based SHAPE National Standards (Standards 2, 3 and 4), and physical activity was measured using three YRBS-derived outcomes: PA Mintues per Day, PA Days per Week, and Fitness Cohort membership. Three regression models were fit for each outcome, with and without demographic covariates. Across all three outcome measures, higher PE knowledge scores were associated with higher levels of physical activity, even after controlling for demographic variables. Standard 2, which corresponds to general fitness knowledge, was the most consistent predictor across models. Effect sizes were small and model fit was poor, suggesting that PE knowledge only explains a small portion of the variance in physical activity behavior. These findings serve as a proof-of-concept for the potential of standards-based surveillance data to inform evidence-based PE curriculum design, and to motivate larger-scale, more representative research.
